status: SEED -- staff-authored from general reference knowledge. 'confidence' is the author's prior; 'verified' stays false until someone checks the cited source (or a scholar / native speaker confirms). Never display an unverified row as fact.
rule: Naming + harmony only (THEME-CATALOG rule). No melody, lyrics or audio. Harmony entries describe conventions of a tradition, credited.

vocab.gloss: tenderly running one's fingers through a loved one's hair
vocab.nuance: A single everyday word for an act of quiet care, given to partners, children and friends alike; often cited as hard to translate in one English word.

vocab.gloss: sweetheart; a deep fondness for someone or something
vocab.nuance: Strongly associated with Northeastern Brazil; used for a beloved person, but also for a favourite place or thing. Its origin is uncertain.
Warm and playful rather than solemn; also used of the closeness between parent and child.

harmony.name: Bossa nova ii-V-I with extended chords
harmony.feel: Cool, intimate and gently bittersweet; seventh and ninth chords voiced softly on nylon-string guitar.
harmony.credit: The bossa nova tradition of late-1950s Rio de Janeiro; exemplified by Antônio Carlos Jobim and João Gilberto (style only).
sources: Ruy Castro, Bossa Nova: The Story of the Brazilian Music That Seduced the World (2000)

harmony.name: Tritone substitution resolving to a major seventh
harmony.feel: A slippery chromatic step into home; sounds sophisticated and tender.
harmony.credit: Jazz harmony convention widely used in bossa nova (style); documented in standard jazz theory texts.
sources: Mark Levine, The Jazz Theory Book (1995)

vocab.gloss: longing for someone or something absent, loved and perhaps lost
vocab.nuance: Holds sweetness and ache together: the presence of an absence. Shared with Brazil and Galicia, and central to Portuguese self-description.

vocab.gloss: to court; to be in a romantic relationship; to spend time as a couple
vocab.nuance: A verb for the shared time of being sweethearts, not only for a feeling.

harmony.name: Fado minor: tonic, subdominant, dominant
harmony.feel: Plaintive and dignified; often described as the sound of saudade.
harmony.credit: Fado tradition of Lisbon and Coimbra (UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, 2011); exemplified by Amália Rodrigues (style only).
sources: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage: Fado, urban popular song of Portugal (2011)

harmony.name: Portuguese guitar over classical guitar accompaniment
harmony.feel: The twelve-string guitarra portuguesa ornaments while the viola keeps a steady harmonic pulse.
harmony.credit: Fado tradition (instrumentation convention).

vocab.gloss: to love (also: to want); everyday affectionate love
vocab.nuance: 'Te quiero' is used widely for family, friends and partners; it is warmer and more everyday than 'te amo'. Usage varies across the Spanish-speaking world.
sources: Diccionario de la lengua española (Real Academia Española)

vocab.nuance: 'Te amo' is often felt as weightier or more solemn than 'te quiero', especially in Spain; in parts of Latin America it is used more freely.
sources: Diccionario de la lengua española (Real Academia Española)

vocab.gloss: one's other half (literally: half an orange)
vocab.nuance: The partner who completes you, imagined as two halves of one fruit.
sources: Diccionario de la lengua española (Real Academia Española)

vocab.gloss: lingering at the table together after a meal, talking
vocab.nuance: Love as unhurried shared time with family and friends.
sources: Diccionario de la lengua española (Real Academia Española)

harmony.name: Andalusian cadence
harmony.feel: A stepwise descent that feels fated, passionate and proud.
harmony.credit: Flamenco and Andalusian tradition (flamenco: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, 2010); term standard in music theory; exemplified by Paco de Lucía (style only).

harmony.name: Phrygian mode (modo de mi / flamenco mode)
harmony.feel: Dark, intense and proud; in practice the third is often raised over the tonic chord, giving the flamenco colour.
harmony.credit: Flamenco tradition; documented in flamenco harmony studies.

vocab.gloss: to hug or cuddle with deep affection; to comfort
vocab.nuance: Widely said to come from Nahuatl 'papachoa' and to mean 'to hug with the soul'; the Nahuatl origin is commonly cited but the poetic 'soul' gloss is a popular folk etymology.
sources: Diccionario de la lengua española (Real Academia Española): apapachar
Diccionario del español de México (El Colegio de México)

vocab.nuance: Used both as a noun for fondness and as a term of address for loved ones.
sources: Diccionario de la lengua española (Real Academia Española)

harmony.name: Ranchera / mariachi major cadence
harmony.feel: Open-hearted, proud and emotional; love declared out loud.
harmony.credit: Mariachi and ranchera tradition (mariachi: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, 2011); exemplified by José Alfredo Jiménez (style only).
sources: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage: Mariachi, string music, song and trumpet (2011)

harmony.name: Romantic bolero turnaround
harmony.feel: Slow, intimate, serenade-like.
harmony.credit: Mexican bolero tradition; exemplified by Agustín Lara and the trios such as Los Panchos (style only).

vocab.nuance: Calls the beloved one's very life; used for partners and children.
sources: Diccionario de la lengua española (Real Academia Española)

vocab.gloss: to love with warm, everyday affection
vocab.nuance: As across the Spanish-speaking world, 'te quiero' covers family, friends and partners.
sources: Diccionario de la lengua española (Real Academia Española)

harmony.name: Cuban bolero ii-V-I
harmony.feel: Tender and unhurried; a serenade in a slow 2/4.
harmony.credit: Cuban trova and bolero tradition of Santiago de Cuba; the early bolero is credited to José 'Pepe' Sánchez (late 19th century).

harmony.name: Son montuno vamp
harmony.feel: Cyclic, warm, dance-inviting; joy that invites everyone in.
harmony.credit: Cuban son tradition; tres guitar and clave; exemplified by Ignacio Piñeiro and Arsenio Rodríguez (style only).

cultures.region: Argentina and Uruguay (Río de la Plata)

vocab.nuance: The usual Latin American verb for missing a loved one (in Spain 'echar de menos' is more common).
sources: Diccionario de la lengua española (Real Academia Española)

vocab.gloss: embrace; in tango, the dance hold itself
vocab.nuance: In tango the embrace is the foundation of the dance: two people moving as one.

harmony.name: Tango minor cadence
harmony.feel: Dramatic, nostalgic and intense; harmonic minor colour with a strong dominant.
harmony.credit: Río de la Plata tango tradition (UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, 2009); exemplified by Carlos Gardel and Astor Piazzolla (style only).

harmony.name: Marcato and bandoneón texture
harmony.feel: Accented beats from the orquesta típica, with the bandoneón's breathing tone.
harmony.credit: Tango orquesta típica convention.

vocab.gloss: the joy of reunion after time apart
vocab.nuance: Names the reunion itself as an event, with the happiness of finding each other again.

vocab.gloss: love at first sight (literally: lightning strike)
vocab.nuance: Sudden, overwhelming attraction or friendship that strikes at once.
Everyday tenderness, used for children, friends and partners.

harmony.name: Impressionist planing (parallel chords)
harmony.feel: Chords that glide in parallel rather than resolving; dreamy, luminous, suspended.
harmony.credit: French Impressionist practice; exemplified by Claude Debussy and Maurice Ravel (style only).

harmony.name: Whole-tone scale
harmony.feel: Weightless and floating; no leading tone pulls it home.
harmony.credit: Used prominently by Claude Debussy (style only).

harmony.name: Bal-musette accordion waltz
harmony.feel: Nostalgic and companionable; a Paris dance-hall sound.
harmony.credit: Parisian bal-musette tradition (accordion).

vocab.gloss: I love you / I care for you (affection)
vocab.nuance: Used for family and friends as well as partners; 'ti amo' is reserved mostly for romantic love.
Weightier and mostly romantic in everyday usage.

vocab.gloss: love at first sight (literally: lightning strike)
vocab.nuance: Sudden, overwhelming attraction.

harmony.name: Neapolitan sixth cadence (bII, usually in first inversion)
harmony.feel: A poignant, darkened approach to the dominant; heartache that turns home.
harmony.credit: Named after the Neapolitan school of the 17th-18th centuries (the attribution of the name is debated); a standard term of Western harmony.

vocab.gloss: the feeling of being safe, sheltered and cared for
vocab.nuance: Combines security, warmth and belonging; often voted among the most beautiful German words.
A counterpart to Einsamkeit (loneliness): the contented solitude of a pair.

vocab.gloss: intense yearning for something far or unattainable
vocab.nuance: Central to German Romanticism; longing with a sense of the infinite.

harmony.name: Romantic chromatic mediant shift
harmony.feel: A sudden change of light without leaving home; wonder and yearning.
harmony.credit: German Romantic Lied practice; exemplified by Franz Schubert and Robert Schumann (style only); theorised in neo-Riemannian theory by Richard Cohn.

cultures.region: United Kingdom, United States and the wider English-speaking world

vocab.gloss: to hold dear and care for tenderly
vocab.nuance: Love as protective care over time.

vocab.gloss: a brief, intense fondness for someone, often unspoken
vocab.nuance: Light and often youthful; the flutter before anything is said.

vocab.gloss: a person who shares your outlook and feelings
vocab.nuance: Friendship-love: recognition and belonging.

harmony.name: '50s / doo-wop progression
harmony.feel: Sweet, sentimental, nostalgic; slow-dance romance.
harmony.credit: Associated with 1950s doo-wop and early rock and roll (style only).

harmony.name: I-V-vi-IV pop progression
harmony.feel: Hopeful, anthemic, uplifting.
harmony.credit: Ubiquitous in Anglophone pop from the 1980s onward (style only).

vocab.nuance: The everyday word for love; also borrowed into Irish English ('she has great grá for him').
A traditional endearment: the beloved as one's very heartbeat.
Affectionate address for partners, children and friends.

harmony.name: Double tonic (alternating I and bVII)
harmony.feel: Swaying, open and timeless; neither chord feels like the final home.
harmony.credit: Irish and Scottish traditional music; the 'double tonic' term is used in Irish traditional music scholarship (e.g. Breandán Breathnach).
sources: Breandán Breathnach, Folk Music and Dances of Ireland (1971)

harmony.name: Dorian mode (common in slow airs)
harmony.feel: Wistful yet hopeful; minor with a brighter sixth.
harmony.credit: Irish traditional slow airs and sean-nós singing (modal practice).

vocab.nuance: The common Gaelic word for love; 'mo ghaol' is 'my love'.
sources: Edward Dwelly, The Illustrated Gaelic-English Dictionary (1901-1911)

vocab.nuance: A warm term of address.
sources: Edward Dwelly, The Illustrated Gaelic-English Dictionary (1901-1911)

vocab.nuance: The sadness of being far from home and one's people.
sources: Edward Dwelly, The Illustrated Gaelic-English Dictionary (1901-1911)

harmony.name: Highland bagpipe scale (Mixolydian on A)
harmony.tuning_note: Our version is a 12-TET approximation; the Great Highland bagpipe chanter uses its own near-just intonation and is pitched well above A440.
harmony.feel: Stirring, outdoor, ancestral.
harmony.credit: Scottish piping tradition.

harmony.name: Drone texture
harmony.feel: A continuous drone beneath everything; steadiness under feeling.
harmony.credit: Scottish piping tradition (drones on tonic and fifth/octave).

vocab.gloss: deep longing for home, a place or a time that may never have been
vocab.nuance: A homesickness mixed with grief and love; central to Welsh identity.
sources: Geiriadur Prifysgol Cymru (University of Wales Dictionary)

vocab.nuance: Both the noun 'love' and a common endearment.
sources: Geiriadur Prifysgol Cymru (University of Wales Dictionary)

vocab.gloss: a cuddle; a safe, cosy place
vocab.nuance: A Welsh English word (from Welsh 'cwtsh'); a hug that also means shelter.

harmony.name: Four-part congregational hymn harmony
harmony.feel: Full, communal, swelling; many voices as one.
harmony.credit: Welsh congregational singing tradition (cymanfa ganu) and male voice choirs.

cultures.care: Hymn singing is part of religious worship for many Welsh communities; described here as a musical texture only.

vocab.nuance: The core noun for love; 'ástin mín' is 'my love'.
Common address ('elskan mín', my darling) for partners and children.
'Ég sakna þín' is 'I miss you'.

harmony.name: Tvísöngur (two-voice singing in parallel fifths)
harmony.feel: Bare, austere, ancient; two voices moving together in open fifths, often crossing.
harmony.credit: Icelandic folk tradition; collected by Bjarni Þorsteinsson in Íslenzk þjóðlög (1906-1909).

vocab.nuance: A mood of shared comfort with people you trust: candles, food, unhurried company. Heavily marketed abroad since the 2010s.
Literally 'dearest'; the everyday word for a girlfriend or boyfriend.

harmony.name: Fællessang (communal song in simple diatonic harmony)
harmony.feel: Everyone singing together from one songbook; belonging made audible.
harmony.credit: Danish folk high school tradition (Højskolesangbogen songbook, inspired by N. F. S. Grundtvig).

vocab.gloss: the euphoric feeling of falling in love
vocab.nuance: The early, giddy stage; distinct from settled love (kjærlighet). Shared with Danish.
Literally 'dearest'.

vocab.gloss: cosy, warm, pleasant in good company
vocab.nuance: A Norwegian cousin of hygge.

harmony.name: Hardanger fiddle scale with raised fourth
harmony.tuning_note: Our version is a 12-TET approximation; in Norwegian folk music the fourth is often a 'neutral' pitch between the perfect and augmented fourth.
harmony.feel: Bright, shimmering, slightly otherworldly.
harmony.credit: Hardingfele tradition; arranged by Edvard Grieg in his Slåtter, Op. 72 (1903) (style reference).

harmony.name: Sympathetic-string resonance
harmony.feel: Unplayed strings ring in response to the played ones; a halo of answering sound.
harmony.credit: Hardingfele construction (sympathetic strings).

vocab.nuance: Applies to people, places and evenings; the warmth of good company.

vocab.gloss: in love (the state of falling in love)
vocab.nuance: The infatuated early stage.
An endearment for partners and children.

harmony.name: Levenslied major cadence
harmony.feel: Sentimental and singalong; heartfelt everyday emotion.
harmony.credit: Dutch levenslied genre (style only).

vocab.nuance: The core noun for love.
'Minulla on ikävä sinua' is 'I miss you'.
A quiet, poetic yearning.

harmony.name: Finnish tango minor cadence
harmony.feel: Melancholy, restrained, deeply felt.
harmony.credit: Finnish tango tradition (mostly in minor keys); exemplified by Unto Mononen and Olavi Virta (style only); celebrated at the Tangomarkkinat festival in Seinäjoki.

harmony.name: Five-string kantele pentachord
harmony.feel: Intimate and ancient; five tones that ring together.
harmony.credit: Traditional Finnish and Karelian kantele tuning.

vocab.nuance: The love between partners; distinct from szeretet.
Broader, caring love, used of family and humanity.

harmony.name: Hungarian minor scale
harmony.feel: Dramatic, exotic to Western ears, yearning.
harmony.credit: A Western theory label linked to 19th-century verbunkos style and to Franz Liszt's usage; Romani musicians were central to that tradition.

harmony.name: Old-style Hungarian folk pentatonic
harmony.feel: Archaic, plain-spoken, rooted.
harmony.credit: Documented by Béla Bartók and Zoltán Kodály in their folk-song collecting.
sources: Béla Bartók, Hungarian Folk Music (1924; English ed. 1931)

cultures.care: The Hungarian minor is sometimes called the 'Gypsy scale'; we avoid that label, which many Roma consider a slur.

vocab.gloss: longing for someone or something loved
vocab.nuance: Often compared with saudade; a cornerstone of Romanian folk poetry and song.
'Mi-e drag de tine' is roughly 'I am fond of you'.

harmony.name: Dorian #4 (common in doina)
harmony.feel: Lamenting, improvised, intimate.
harmony.credit: Romanian doina tradition (UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, 2009); collected by Béla Bartók.

harmony.name: Free-rhythm (parlando rubato) song
harmony.feel: Unmetred and speech-like, following breath and feeling.
harmony.credit: Romanian doina tradition; term 'parlando rubato' from Bartók's analyses.

vocab.gloss: longing; missing someone or a place
vocab.nuance: Ranges from missing a person to a nostalgic ache for home.
The most common Polish endearment.
The core noun for love.

harmony.name: Lydian mode (raised fourth, Podhale)
harmony.feel: Bright and bracing, mountain air.
harmony.credit: Podhale highland (Górale) folk music; Lydian inflections also in the mazurkas of Frédéric Chopin and Karol Szymanowski (style only).

harmony.name: Mazurka triple-meter accent
harmony.feel: A lilting triple meter with accents falling off the first beat.
harmony.credit: Polish mazurka folk dance tradition; exemplified by Frédéric Chopin (style only).

vocab.nuance: Usually reserved for love between partners.
sources: Slovnyk ukrainskoi movy (Academic Dictionary of the Ukrainian Language)

vocab.nuance: Wider than kokhannia; the exact boundary between the two is debated among speakers.
sources: Slovnyk ukrainskoi movy (Academic Dictionary of the Ukrainian Language)

harmony.name: Ukrainian Dorian
harmony.feel: Plaintive and searching; minor with a raised fourth.
harmony.credit: Ukrainian folk tradition; the name is used in klezmer and folk-music scholarship.

harmony.name: Folk polyphonic choral singing
harmony.feel: Open-throated multi-part singing; communal and powerful.
harmony.credit: Ukrainian village polyphonic singing tradition.

vocab.nuance: Famously described by Vladimir Nabokov as having no single English equivalent; ranges from boredom to deep yearning.
sources: Vladimir Nabokov, translation and commentary of Pushkin's Eugene Onegin (1964)

vocab.nuance: The core noun, for all kinds of love.
Gentle, caring love.

harmony.name: Russian romance minor cadence
harmony.feel: Heartfelt, melancholy, intimate salon feeling.
harmony.credit: Russian romance (romans) tradition; exemplified by Alexander Alyabyev and Mikhail Glinka (style only).

vocab.nuance: One of four Greek words often contrasted; the neat four-way scheme was popularised by C. S. Lewis and is partly modern.
sources: C. S. Lewis, The Four Loves (1960)

vocab.nuance: Modern Greek 'agápi' is the ordinary word for love; 'agape' as selfless love comes largely from Christian theology.
sources: C. S. Lewis, The Four Loves (1960)

vocab.nuance: Love as loyalty and companionship.
The natural love of parents and children.

vocab.gloss: doing something with soul, care and love
vocab.nuance: From Turkish 'merak'; popular explanations online sometimes romanticise it beyond everyday usage.
sources: Babiniotis, Lexiko tis Neas Ellinikis Glossas

harmony.name: Rebetiko dromos Hijaz
harmony.tuning_note: On fretted bouzouki the dromoi are played in 12-TET; their makam ancestors use microtonal intervals.
harmony.feel: Longing, smoky, intense.
harmony.credit: Rebetiko tradition (dromoi derived from Ottoman makam); exemplified by Markos Vamvakaris and Vassilis Tsitsanis (style only).

harmony.name: Rebetiko dromos Hijazkiar
harmony.tuning_note: On fretted bouzouki played in 12-TET; makam ancestors are microtonal.
harmony.feel: Exotic and dramatic, with an augmented step on both halves.
harmony.credit: Rebetiko tradition (style only).

cultures.care: Agape also has specific theological meaning in Christianity; we present it as a word, not a doctrine.

vocab.nuance: Via Turkish 'sevda' from Arabic 'sawdā'' (black bile, melancholy); gives its name to the sevdalinka song tradition.
A Turkish loanword (aşık) used in Bosnian song culture.

harmony.name: Hijaz-type scale in sevdalinka
harmony.tuning_note: Our version is a 12-TET approximation; older performances can carry makam-derived intonation.
harmony.feel: Slow, ornamented, heart-heavy.
harmony.credit: Sevdalinka tradition; exemplified by Himzo Polovina and Safet Isović (style only).

vocab.nuance: Also used of mystical love in Sufi poetry.
sources: Türk Dil Kurumu, Güncel Türkçe Sözlük

vocab.nuance: From Arabic 'sawdā'' (black bile, melancholy); love tinged with longing.
sources: Türk Dil Kurumu, Güncel Türkçe Sözlük

vocab.gloss: longing for someone or somewhere far away
vocab.nuance: The ache of separation.
sources: Türk Dil Kurumu, Güncel Türkçe Sözlük

vocab.gloss: heart, as the seat of affection and desire
vocab.nuance: Distinct from the anatomical heart (kalp); 'gönül vermek' is to give one's heart.
sources: Türk Dil Kurumu, Güncel Türkçe Sözlük

harmony.name: Makam Hicaz
harmony.tuning_note: Our version is a 12-TET approximation; Turkish makam theory (Arel-Ezgi-Uzdilek) divides the whole tone into commas, so the second and third degrees differ from equal temperament.
harmony.feel: Longing and yearning; widely heard in love songs.
harmony.credit: Ottoman/Turkish makam tradition; documented by Karl Signell.
sources: Karl Signell, Makam: Modal Practice in Turkish Art Music (1977)

harmony.name: Makam Uşşak
harmony.tuning_note: Our version is a 12-TET approximation; the second degree (segah) lies between a semitone and a whole tone; we round it down.
harmony.feel: Tender, intimate; its name means 'lovers'.
harmony.credit: Ottoman/Turkish makam tradition.
sources: Karl Signell, Makam: Modal Practice in Turkish Art Music (1977)

vocab.nuance: The core noun for love.
Shared with Persian and other regional languages; 'Ani jan' = dear Ani.
Especially the longing of separation and diaspora.

harmony.name: Duduk melody over a sustained drone (dam)
harmony.tuning_note: The duduk is a double-reed instrument with its own intonation; the drone is not tied to 12-TET.
harmony.feel: Mournful, warm, breath-like; one player sustains the drone while another sings out.
harmony.credit: Armenian duduk tradition (UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, 2008); exemplified by Djivan Gasparyan (style only).
sources: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage: Duduk and its music (2008)

vocab.nuance: The core noun for love.

vocab.gloss: 'I would take your place'; dear, darling
vocab.nuance: Endearment implying you would bear another's suffering for them; the literal gloss is widely given but nuance varies by speaker.

harmony.name: Three-part polyphony with open fifths and drone
harmony.tuning_note: Traditional Georgian tuning is not 12-TET and is debated by scholars; our version is an approximation.
harmony.feel: Resonant, ancient, communal; voices meeting on open fifths and unisons.
harmony.credit: Georgian polyphonic singing (UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, 2008); studied by Joseph Jordania.
sources: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage: Georgian polyphonic singing (2008)
Joseph Jordania, Who Asked the First Question? (2006)

cultures.care: Much Georgian polyphony is liturgical (Orthodox chant); described here as texture only.

vocab.nuance: The core word for love, ancient and modern.
A central ethical and religious concept: love expressed through kind deeds.
Calling someone 'my soul' in everyday Israeli speech.

harmony.name: Ahava Rabbah prayer mode
harmony.feel: Yearning, intense, devotional.
harmony.credit: Ashkenazi synagogue prayer-mode (nusach) tradition, named after a prayer; documented by A. Z. Idelsohn.
sources: A. Z. Idelsohn, Jewish Music in Its Historical Development (1929)

harmony.name: Adonai Malakh prayer mode
harmony.feel: Majestic and bright, with a lowered seventh.
harmony.credit: Ashkenazi nusach tradition, named after a prayer; documented by A. Z. Idelsohn.
sources: A. Z. Idelsohn, Jewish Music in Its Historical Development (1929)

cultures.care: Chesed and the prayer modes are religious concepts; named respectfully and described factually, never applied to sacred texts or chant.

vocab.gloss: destined; one's destined partner or match
vocab.nuance: Also used of fated friendships or events.
sources: Uriel Weinreich, Modern English-Yiddish Yiddish-English Dictionary (1968)

vocab.nuance: The glow of seeing loved ones flourish.
sources: Uriel Weinreich, Modern English-Yiddish Yiddish-English Dictionary (1968)

harmony.name: Mi Sheberakh / altered Dorian (klezmer)
harmony.feel: Searching and plaintive; a minor mode with a raised fourth.
harmony.credit: Klezmer tradition; mode named after a prayer.

harmony.name: Freygish chord movement (I, iv, bvii)
harmony.feel: Bittersweet dance harmony built from the freygish (Phrygian dominant) mode.
harmony.credit: Klezmer accompaniment tradition (style only).

cultures.care: Several klezmer mode names come from synagogue prayers; named respectfully.

cultures.region: Arab world (North Africa and Western Asia)

vocab.nuance: The general, everyday word for love.
sources: Hans Wehr, A Dictionary of Modern Written Arabic (1961)

vocab.nuance: Intense love; in Sufi poetry also love of the divine.
sources: Hans Wehr, A Dictionary of Modern Written Arabic (1961)

vocab.nuance: Often listed among the 'stages of love' in later Arabic writing; popular lists of dozens of 'Arabic words for love' simplify the sources.
sources: Hans Wehr, A Dictionary of Modern Written Arabic (1961)

vocab.nuance: Common in song and poetry for deep attachment.
sources: Hans Wehr, A Dictionary of Modern Written Arabic (1961)

harmony.name: Maqam Bayati
harmony.tuning_note: Our version is a 12-TET approximation; the second degree is a half-flat (about 150 cents above the tonic), which we round down to a semitone.
harmony.feel: Warm, earthy, tender; one of the most common maqamat.
harmony.credit: Arab maqam tradition (discussed at the 1932 Cairo Congress of Arab Music); exemplified by Umm Kulthum and Mohammed Abdel Wahab (style only).
sources: Johnny Farraj & Sami Abu Shumays, Inside Arabic Music (2019)
Habib Hassan Touma, The Music of the Arabs (1996)

harmony.name: Maqam Hijaz
harmony.tuning_note: Our version is a 12-TET approximation; intonation of the augmented second varies by region and performer; the upper jins can also vary.
harmony.feel: Longing, distance, the desert.
harmony.credit: Arab maqam tradition.
sources: Johnny Farraj & Sami Abu Shumays, Inside Arabic Music (2019)

harmony.name: Maqam Saba
harmony.tuning_note: Our version is a 12-TET approximation; the second degree is a half-flat and the scale does not repeat at the octave (its upper octave is lowered), which 12-TET cannot fully show.
harmony.feel: Grief and sorrow; heartache.
harmony.credit: Arab maqam tradition.
sources: Johnny Farraj & Sami Abu Shumays, Inside Arabic Music (2019)

cultures.care: 'Ishq also carries Sufi devotional meaning; some maqamat are used in Qur'anic recitation, which we never imitate.

vocab.nuance: Central to classical Persian poetry (Rumi, Hafez), both human and divine.
The everyday word for missing a loved one.
A tender address and a warm way of answering someone who calls your name.

harmony.name: Dastgah Shur
harmony.tuning_note: Our version is a 12-TET approximation; the second degree is a koron (roughly quarter-tone flat), rounded down here.
harmony.feel: Introspective, longing; the 'mother' of many melodic modes.
harmony.credit: Persian radif tradition (UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, 2009), codified by Mirza Abdollah; analysed by Hormoz Farhat.
sources: Hormoz Farhat, The Dastgah Concept in Persian Music (1990)
Ella Zonis, Classical Persian Music: An Introduction (1973)

harmony.name: Dastgah Homayun
harmony.tuning_note: Our version is a 12-TET approximation; the second degree is a koron, rounded down here.
harmony.feel: Grand and passionate.
harmony.credit: Persian radif tradition; analysed by Hormoz Farhat.
sources: Hormoz Farhat, The Dastgah Concept in Persian Music (1990)

vocab.nuance: The everyday word for love, for partners, family and friends.
From Sanskrit prema; also devotional love.
From Arabic via Persian/Urdu; common in film song and poetry.

vocab.gloss: the pain of separation from the beloved
vocab.nuance: A major theme of Indian poetry, including bhakti devotional love for the divine.

harmony.name: Raga Yaman (Kalyan thaat)
harmony.tuning_note: Our version is a 12-TET approximation; ragas are sung against a drone with flexible intonation, and a raga is more than its scale (characteristic phrases, ascent and descent rules).
harmony.feel: Serene, romantic, evening devotion.
harmony.credit: Hindustani classical tradition; thaat classification by V. N. Bhatkhande (early 20th century).
sources: Walter Kaufmann, The Ragas of North India (1968)

harmony.name: Raga Bhairavi (Bhairavi thaat)
harmony.tuning_note: Our version is a 12-TET approximation; intonation is flexible and the raga allows additional notes in practice.
harmony.feel: Devotional pathos; traditionally closes a concert.
harmony.credit: Hindustani classical tradition; thaat classification by V. N. Bhatkhande.
sources: Walter Kaufmann, The Ragas of North India (1968)

cultures.care: Viraha and prem also belong to bhakti devotion; ragas carry spiritual meaning for many practitioners.

vocab.nuance: The common Urdu word for love, from Arabic.
sources: John T. Platts, A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi and English (1884)

vocab.nuance: A core theme of the ghazal.
sources: John T. Platts, A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi and English (1884)

vocab.nuance: The counterpart of hijr in ghazal poetry.
sources: John T. Platts, A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi and English (1884)

harmony.name: Ghazal performance texture
harmony.tuning_note: Raga-based; intonation follows Hindustani practice, not 12-TET.
harmony.feel: Intimate, reflective; harmonium and tabla support a poet's couplets.
harmony.credit: Ghazal tradition; poets Mir Taqi Mir and Mirza Ghalib; singers Begum Akhtar and Mehdi Hassan (style only).

harmony.name: Khamaj thaat (light-classical colour)
harmony.tuning_note: Our version is a 12-TET approximation; intonation follows Hindustani practice.
harmony.feel: Playful-romantic, light-classical.
harmony.credit: Hindustani tradition; thaat by V. N. Bhatkhande; common in thumri and ghazal.
sources: Walter Kaufmann, The Ragas of North India (1968)

cultures.region: Tamil Nadu (India), Sri Lanka and the Tamil diaspora

vocab.nuance: The word for love between partners; ancient Sangam poetry calls the love genre 'akam' (the inner world).
Broad, caring love; the Thirukkural devotes a chapter to it.

harmony.name: Kalyani (65th melakarta)
harmony.tuning_note: Our version is a 12-TET approximation; Carnatic music uses gamaka (oscillation) and flexible intonation.
harmony.feel: Auspicious, bright, devotional and romantic.
harmony.credit: Carnatic tradition; 72-melakarta scheme from Venkatamakhin's Chaturdandi Prakashika (17th century).

harmony.name: Kharaharapriya (22nd melakarta)
harmony.tuning_note: Our version is a 12-TET approximation; gamaka and intonation are not captured.
harmony.feel: Deep, compassionate, contemplative.
harmony.credit: Carnatic tradition; Venkatamakhin's melakarta scheme.

harmony.name: Mohanam (pentatonic)
harmony.tuning_note: Our version is a 12-TET approximation; gamaka not captured.
harmony.feel: Joyful, tender, widely loved.
harmony.credit: Carnatic tradition; janya of Harikambhoji (28th melakarta).

vocab.nuance: Literally 'good dwelling'; the everyday word for love.
In Bengali everyday usage, the bond of affection toward people, animals and places; in philosophy the same word means 'illusion'.

harmony.name: Rabindra Sangeet
harmony.tuning_note: Raga-based intonation, not 12-TET.
harmony.feel: Lyrical, contemplative, drawing on raga, kirtan and baul folk.
harmony.credit: Songs of Rabindranath Tagore (1861-1941), a defining Bengali genre (style only).

vocab.nuance: In bhakti traditions, the highest love for the divine.
Central in Buddhism and Hinduism; one of the four Buddhist brahmavihāras.
Pali 'mettā'; goodwill toward all beings, another brahmavihāra.

harmony.name: Vedic recitation with pitch accents
harmony.tuning_note: Recited with three pitch accents (udātta, anudātta, svarita) that are not 12-TET pitches.
harmony.feel: Steady, ancient, meditative.
harmony.credit: Tradition of Vedic chanting (UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, 2008).
sources: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage: Tradition of Vedic Chanting (2008)

cultures.care: These are sacred concepts in Hindu, Buddhist and Jain traditions, and Vedic chanting is ritual practice: described factually, never imitated or remixed.

cultures.region: China, Taiwan and Chinese communities worldwide

vocab.nuance: The core word for love; spoken directly less often than in English, with love shown through care.
The sense that a bond was meant to be; from Buddhist ideas of conditioned connection.

vocab.gloss: heartache on someone's behalf; to dote on
vocab.nuance: Literally 'heart-ache'; the feeling of pain for a loved one's hardship, expressing deep care.

vocab.gloss: to miss; to think of with longing
vocab.nuance: Longing for an absent loved one.

harmony.name: Gong mode (major pentatonic)
harmony.feel: Open, balanced, bright.
harmony.credit: Chinese pentatonic modal theory (five modes: gong, shang, jue, zhi, yu).

harmony.name: Yu mode (minor pentatonic)
harmony.feel: Plaintive, tender, nostalgic.
harmony.credit: Chinese pentatonic modal theory.

harmony.name: Canon-style progression (common in Mandopop)
harmony.feel: Warm, nostalgic, gently uplifting.
harmony.credit: Derived from the bass pattern of Johann Pachelbel's Canon (c. 1700); very common in Mandopop ballads (style only).

vocab.gloss: to like; to be fond of
vocab.nuance: The everyday way to say you like or love someone, gentler than 'oi3' (愛).
Colloquial Cantonese for cherishing someone; also used for a kiss.

harmony.name: Cantopop ballad progression
harmony.feel: Lush and bittersweet; in Cantopop the song's tones must also fit the language's tones.
harmony.credit: Cantopop ballad tradition (style only).

vocab.nuance: Often longing for someone, the early or unfulfilled stage.
Broader and deeper than koi; also love for family and humanity.
Popularised in psychology by Takeo Doi (The Anatomy of Dependence, 1971); the trust that you can lean on someone's care.
sources: Takeo Doi, Amae no Kōzō (The Anatomy of Dependence) (1971)

vocab.gloss: the premonition of falling in love
vocab.nuance: A sense on meeting someone that love will come; viral 'untranslatable' lists sometimes overstate how special the phrase is.
A sweet ache of love or loss.

harmony.name: Royal road progression (Ōdō shinkō)
harmony.feel: Wistful, emotional, bittersweet hope; a J-pop staple.
harmony.credit: Common in J-pop and anime music; widely discussed by Japanese music commentators (style only).

harmony.name: Yonanuki major (major pentatonic)
harmony.feel: Simple, nostalgic, bright.
harmony.credit: Japanese term ('without the 4th and 7th') from Meiji-era music education.

harmony.name: Miyako-bushi scale
harmony.tuning_note: Our version is a 12-TET approximation; traditional instruments such as koto and shamisen are not tied to equal temperament.
harmony.feel: Austere, melancholic, traditional.
harmony.credit: Japanese traditional music; tetrachord theory by Koizumi Fumio (1958).
sources: Koizumi Fumio, Nihon dentō ongaku no kenkyū (1958)

vocab.gloss: deep affection and attachment built over shared time
vocab.nuance: Grows slowly between family, friends, neighbours and even rivals.
sources: Standard Korean Language Dictionary (National Institute of Korean Language)

vocab.nuance: The flutter of anticipation, often in new love.
sources: Standard Korean Language Dictionary (National Institute of Korean Language)

vocab.gloss: longing for someone or something missed
vocab.nuance: A tender, aching nostalgia.
sources: Standard Korean Language Dictionary (National Institute of Korean Language)

harmony.name: Yonanuki minor pentatonic (trot)
harmony.feel: Melancholy and sentimental.
harmony.credit: Korean trot (teuroteu) tradition, historically linked to Japanese enka; exemplified by Lee Mi-ja and Nam Jin (style only).

harmony.name: Final-chorus upward key change
harmony.feel: Lifts emotion at the climax.
harmony.credit: A common convention in K-ballads (and in pop worldwide) (style only).

vocab.nuance: The word for romantic love.
sources: Từ điển tiếng Việt (Hoàng Phê, ed.)

vocab.gloss: to love tenderly; to care, to pity
vocab.nuance: Love with compassion; used for family, partners and anyone one cares for.
sources: Từ điển tiếng Việt (Hoàng Phê, ed.)

vocab.nuance: 'Anh nhớ em' is 'I miss you'.
sources: Từ điển tiếng Việt (Hoàng Phê, ed.)

harmony.name: Quan họ antiphonal duet singing
harmony.tuning_note: Traditional Vietnamese vocal intonation is not tied to 12-TET.
harmony.feel: Call and response between groups of men and women; friendship and courtship.
harmony.credit: Quan họ Bắc Ninh folk songs (UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, 2009).
sources: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage: Quan Họ Bắc Ninh folk songs (2009)

vocab.nuance: The rush you feel, or feel for others, in a romantic moment.
The core word for love, from 'ibig' (to want, to love).
A poetic endearment.

harmony.name: Kundiman: minor opening, parallel-major close
harmony.feel: From longing into hope.
harmony.credit: Filipino kundiman art-song tradition; exemplified by Francisco Santiago and Nicanor Abelardo (style only).

vocab.nuance: Shared with Malay.
Love that cares; also used as an endearment.
Gentle love; 'terima kasih' (thank you) literally 'receive love'.

harmony.name: Slendro (gamelan five-tone tuning)
harmony.tuning_note: Slendro has five near-equal steps of about 240 cents, and every gamelan set has its own tuning; no 12-TET fit is faithful, so ours is a rough approximation.
harmony.feel: Calm, flowing, communal.
harmony.credit: Javanese and Balinese gamelan tradition (gamelan: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, 2021).

harmony.name: Pelog (gamelan seven-tone tuning, five-tone subset)
harmony.tuning_note: Pelog intervals are unequal and vary by ensemble; this 12-TET subset is only an approximation.
harmony.feel: Deep, solemn, mysterious.
harmony.credit: Javanese and Balinese gamelan tradition.

harmony.name: Keroncong interlocking strings
harmony.feel: Gentle, nostalgic; small plucked lutes interlock over plucked cello.
harmony.credit: Keroncong tradition with Portuguese roots; exemplified by Gesang Martohartono (style only).

vocab.nuance: The core noun for love.

vocab.gloss: consideration; not wanting to burden others
vocab.nuance: A form of care shown through restraint and respect.

harmony.name: Thai classical scale (pentatonic in use)
harmony.tuning_note: Thai classical tuning divides the octave into seven roughly equal steps (about 171 cents); our pentatonic 12-TET version is an approximation.
harmony.feel: Graceful and serene.
harmony.credit: Thai classical tradition (piphat ensembles).

vocab.nuance: The core noun for love, family and romantic.

vocab.gloss: homeland; the land where one belongs
vocab.nuance: Deep attachment to the land of one's birth and kin.

harmony.name: Urtyn duu (long song)
harmony.tuning_note: Traditional intonation is not tied to 12-TET.
harmony.feel: Spacious, melismatic, free-rhythm; the open steppe.
harmony.credit: Mongolian long song tradition (UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, 2008, Mongolia and China).
sources: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage: Urtiin Duu (2008)

harmony.name: Khöömii overtone singing over a drone
harmony.tuning_note: Overtones follow the harmonic series, not 12-TET.
harmony.feel: One voice sounding two layers at once; awe and wind.
harmony.credit: Mongolian khöömei tradition (UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, 2010).
sources: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage: Mongolian art of singing, Khöömei (2010)

vocab.nuance: A word and a way of life. The popular etymology 'alo' (presence) + 'hā' (breath) is a folk etymology without scholarly support.
sources: Mary Kawena Pukui & Samuel H. Elbert, Hawaiian Dictionary (1986)

vocab.nuance: A tender term of address.
sources: Mary Kawena Pukui & Samuel H. Elbert, Hawaiian Dictionary (1986)

vocab.nuance: Includes chosen family and the duty of care between them.
sources: Mary Kawena Pukui & Samuel H. Elbert, Hawaiian Dictionary (1986)

harmony.name: Hawaiian vamp
harmony.feel: Gentle, swaying, an invitation home.
harmony.credit: Hawaiian popular song tradition (the vamp between verses).

harmony.name: Kī hōʻalu (slack key guitar)
harmony.feel: Open tunings, alternating bass with ringing strings; warm and relaxed.
harmony.credit: Hawaiian slack key tradition; exemplified by Gabby Pahinui (style only).

cultures.care: Aloha carries cultural and spiritual weight for Native Hawaiians; it is offered here with respect, not as a brand.

vocab.nuance: A broad love that includes care for others and the community.
sources: Te Aka Māori Dictionary (John C. Moorfield)

vocab.gloss: kinship; a sense of family connection
vocab.nuance: Relationships built through shared experience and belonging.
sources: Te Aka Māori Dictionary (John C. Moorfield)

vocab.nuance: Showing respect by caring for guests and kin.
sources: Te Aka Māori Dictionary (John C. Moorfield)

harmony.name: Waiata-ā-ringa (action song) major harmony
harmony.feel: Communal, joyful, guitar-led singing.
harmony.credit: Modern Māori action song tradition, developed in the 20th century (e.g. by Tuini Ngāwai and Sir Āpirana Ngata).

cultures.care: Waiata and their associated tikanga (customs) belong to iwi and hapū; some waiata are tapu (sacred) and not to be reused.

vocab.nuance: Related to Hawaiian aloha and Māori aroha.
The basis of fa'a Sāmoa (the Samoan way).

harmony.name: Samoan choral four-part singing
harmony.feel: Rich, resonant, communal.
harmony.credit: Samoan choral tradition (church and community choirs).

cultures.care: Much Samoan choral singing is part of church worship; described as texture only.

vocab.nuance: Also used in Andean philosophy for loving will; spelling and use vary across varieties.
sources: Diccionario Quechua-Español-Quechua (Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, 2005)

vocab.gloss: to love tenderly; to care for
vocab.nuance: Tender, caring love, also for family.
sources: Diccionario Quechua-Español-Quechua (Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, 2005)

vocab.nuance: Also spelled sonqo; seat of feeling and love.
sources: Diccionario Quechua-Español-Quechua (Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, 2005)

harmony.name: Huayno minor pentatonic
harmony.feel: Bittersweet, high and clear; dance and longing together.
harmony.credit: Andean huayno tradition.

harmony.name: Yaraví (slow lament-love song)
harmony.feel: Slow, melancholy; love and separation.
harmony.credit: Andean yaraví tradition, descended from the pre-Hispanic harawi; associated with poet Mariano Melgar (early 19th century).

vocab.gloss: 'all my relatives'; we are all related
vocab.nuance: A prayer phrase expressing kinship with all beings.

vocab.gloss: I love you / I cherish you
vocab.nuance: Spelling varies (e.g. 'techihila').

harmony.name: Plains drum-group song texture
harmony.tuning_note: Not 12-TET; there is no chordal harmony.
harmony.feel: Heartbeat-like drum with singers; communal power.
harmony.credit: Northern Plains song traditions, including powwow drum groups.

cultures.care: 'Mitákuye oyás'iŋ' is a prayer phrase and many songs are ceremonial or owned; we describe, never reproduce or commercialise, them.

vocab.nuance: The everyday verb for love.
A tender adjective of affection.

harmony.name: Joik (luohti)
harmony.tuning_note: Joik intonation is not tied to 12-TET.
harmony.feel: A joik is sung 'of' a person or place, not 'about' it; recalling a loved one into presence.
harmony.credit: Sámi joik tradition.

cultures.care: A personal joik belongs to the person it is for; joik was suppressed historically and is sacred to many Sámi.

vocab.nuance: Love in general: family, friendship, community.
Love between partners.
Used as a term of endearment.

harmony.name: Taarab orchestra texture
harmony.tuning_note: Taarab draws on Arab maqam intonation; our version is an approximation.
harmony.feel: Elegant, poetic love song with oud, violins and qanun.
harmony.credit: Zanzibari and coastal taarab tradition; exemplified by Siti binti Saad (style only).

vocab.nuance: The core noun for love.
sources: A Dictionary of the Yoruba Language (Church Missionary Society, 1913)

vocab.nuance: Literally 'one who loves'.
sources: A Dictionary of the Yoruba Language (Church Missionary Society, 1913)

harmony.name: Jùjú: talking drum and interlocking guitars
harmony.feel: Celebratory, layered, communal praise and joy.
harmony.credit: Nigerian jùjú tradition; exemplified by I. K. Dairo and King Sunny Adé (style only).
sources: Christopher Waterman, Jùjú: A Social History and Ethnography of an African Popular Music (1990)

vocab.nuance: The common noun for love.
Literally 'child of mother'; extends to kinsfolk and solidarity.

harmony.name: Igbo highlife major cadence
harmony.feel: Easy, joyful, conversational guitar music.
harmony.credit: Igbo highlife tradition; exemplified by Chief Stephen Osita Osadebe (style only).

vocab.nuance: The core noun; 'me dɔ wo' is 'I love you'.
Used as an endearment.

harmony.name: Highlife major cadence
harmony.feel: Bright, swinging, celebratory dance music.
harmony.credit: Ghanaian highlife; dance-band highlife exemplified by E. T. Mensah, 'King of Highlife' (style only).

cultures.region: Democratic Republic of the Congo and Republic of the Congo

vocab.nuance: The core noun; also a common term of endearment in song.
Seat of feeling.

harmony.name: Congolese rumba cyclic cadence
harmony.feel: Smooth, sweet, dance-inviting.
harmony.credit: Congolese rumba (UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, 2021); exemplified by Franco Luambo and Tabu Ley Rochereau (style only).
sources: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage: Congolese rumba (2021)
Gary Stewart, Rumba on the River (2000)

harmony.name: Sebene interlocking guitars
harmony.feel: An extended, cyclic guitar dance section; joy and release.
harmony.credit: Congolese rumba and soukous tradition.
sources: Gary Stewart, Rumba on the River (2000)

vocab.nuance: The core noun for love.
Also the name of a song genre and a qenet (mode).

harmony.name: Qenet Tizita (major)
harmony.tuning_note: Our version is a 12-TET approximation; intonation of Ethiopian qenet varies by region and performer.
harmony.feel: Nostalgic, longing, tender.
harmony.credit: Ethiopian qenet system; exemplified by Mulatu Astatke and Mahmoud Ahmed (style only).

harmony.name: Qenet Bati (major)
harmony.tuning_note: Our version is a 12-TET approximation; intonation varies.
harmony.feel: Bright and spacious.
harmony.credit: Ethiopian qenet system.

harmony.name: Qenet Ambassel
harmony.tuning_note: Our version is a 12-TET approximation; intonation varies.
harmony.feel: Solemn and dark.
harmony.credit: Ethiopian qenet system.

vocab.nuance: The core noun for love.
From Arabic; friendship-love.

harmony.name: Qaraami love-song style (oud-led)
harmony.tuning_note: Somali music is largely pentatonic; intonation not tied to 12-TET.
harmony.feel: Gentle, poetic love songs.
harmony.credit: Somali qaraami tradition (mid-20th century); Abdullahi Qarshe is often credited as a founding figure (style only).

vocab.nuance: The core noun for love.
sources: Doke, Malcolm & Sikakana, English-Zulu Zulu-English Dictionary (1990)

vocab.gloss: humanity toward others; 'a person is a person through other people'
vocab.nuance: Shared across Nguni languages; personhood grounded in community and care.
sources: Doke, Malcolm & Sikakana, English-Zulu Zulu-English Dictionary (1990)

harmony.name: Isicathamiya choral cadence
harmony.feel: Soft, warm, close-harmony.
harmony.credit: Zulu isicathamiya a cappella tradition; exemplified by Solomon Linda and Ladysmith Black Mambazo (style only).
sources: Veit Erlmann, Nightsong: Performance, Power, and Practice in South Africa (1996)

harmony.name: A cappella male choral close harmony
harmony.feel: Bass-heavy, gentle, communal.
harmony.credit: Isicathamiya tradition.
sources: Veit Erlmann, Nightsong: Performance, Power, and Practice in South Africa (1996)

vocab.nuance: Related to saudade.
Warm care.

harmony.name: Gaita (bagpipe) drone
harmony.tuning_note: Gaita chanters have their own tuning; 12-TET is an approximation.
harmony.feel: Steady, festive, ancestral.
harmony.credit: Galician gaita tradition.

vocab.nuance: Thumb, index and little finger extended, combining I, L and Y; widely used in Deaf culture and beyond.
Commonly signed with crossed fists over the chest.

cultures.care: Signs vary regionally; learn them from Deaf signers. Sign languages are full languages, not gestures.
